tier_rationale: Sonos's own support documentation states plainly that creating a Sonos account is required the first time a Sonos system is set up, and the system-requirements page separately requires a high-speed internet connection and a smartphone running the Sonos app to complete setup — an account mandatory at setup is a REJECT trigger on its own under the decision table, independent of anything the bar does afterward.
rejection_reason: Setup cannot be completed without creating or logging into a Sonos account, and the app used to do that setup requires the device to be online. There is no path to first use that skips the account.
the_unplug_test: This soundbar cannot be turned into a usable product without first going through the Sonos app and a Sonos account, which itself requires an internet connection to complete. Once set up it plays optical audio from a TV, but there is no way to get from box to working speaker with the router off, and no documented offline first-run path exists.
offline_losses: Initial setup cannot be completed at all without the Sonos app and a Sonos account, which itself requires internet access.

sources.supports: Sonos's own support article states that when setting up a Sonos system for the first time, the owner will be required to create an account; no path to skip this is documented.

Sonos's own system-requirements page lists a high-speed wired internet connection, a Wi-Fi router, and an iOS/Android device running the Sonos app as required to set up a Sonos system, corroborating that setup is not achievable offline.
Manufacturer product page confirms current model, connectivity (optical, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth for setup handoff) and price ($279) for the Ray soundbar.

alternatives.why: A soundbar at a comparable price with a wireless subwoofer, HDMI-ARC and optical inputs, Bluetooth streaming, and a full setup and firmware-update path documented start to finish with no app and no account of any kind.

open_questions: Did not verify whether a Sonos soundbar retains any function if the account is later deleted or Sonos suspends it post-setup — out of scope for this rejection, which rests on the setup gate alone, but worth a follow-up record if Sonos's cloud dependency for day-to-day playback is characterized in detail.

Radios list (wifi, ble) is Sonos's generally-documented connectivity for this product line; not independently confirmed against an FCC grant for this run, since the rejection turns on the account-at-setup fact, not on the radio inventory.
notes: Sonos is a vendor-ledger candidate, not scored here per this run's brief (vendor_risk left at 0; scoring is the orchestrator's call). Documented incidents worth adding to data/vendors.json, each with its own source: (1) the 2019 'Recycle Mode' trade-up program that permanently bricked working speakers traded in for a discount, reversed after backlash in early 2020 (Engadget, What Hi-Fi, Consumer Reports coverage); (2) the 2020 announcement (partially reversed) that 'legacy' Sonos products would stop receiving software updates, raised by owners as an effective end-of-support date for hardware that still worked; (3) the May 2024 Sonos app rewrite, which shipped with missing core features (alarms, local music library browsing, playlist editing) and connectivity regressions on already-purchased hardware, leading to a federal class-action suit (Goodrow v. Sonos, filed June 2025) and roughly $500M of market-value loss cited in coverage of the CEO's departure.

changelog.change: vendor_risk raised 0 -> 3 when Sonos was added to the ledger with three dated incidents. The tier is unchanged and was never affected: REJECT rests on the account being mandatory at setup, which is a fact about the device, not about the vendor's conduct.
